label: Formulated the doctrine of universal care (jian'ai) and early consequentialism
description: Mozi formulated jian'ai (universal mutual care) as an objective normative standard, arguing that social turmoil stems from partiality and can only be cured by impartial benevolence toward all people.
historicalContext: Articulated during the Warring States period in response to pervasive interstate warfare and social disintegration across the Central Plains of China.
dialecticalTension: Opposes Confucian graded love (qinqin) which prioritizes familial kinship above strangers and foreign states.

citations.author: Mozi
citations.quote: If everyone in the world loves universally, treating others' countries as their own, who would invade them? There would be no wars.

citations.author: Chris Fraser
citations.work: The Philosophy of the Mozi: The First Consequentialists in Chinese Thought

label: Critiqued Confucian ritualism and partial filial devotion
description: Mozi was originally trained in the Confucian tradition but broke away, condemning Confucian lavish funerals, extended mourning rituals, and kinship partiality as wasteful and harmful to the common welfare.
historicalContext: The earliest and most formidable philosophical counter-movement against orthodox early Confucianism during the 5th century BCE.
dialecticalTension: Pits Confucian aesthetic ritualism (li) and filial partiality against Mohist utilitarian thrift and universal impartial care.

citations.author: Mozi
citations.quote: The Confucians corrupt people with elaborate rituals and bankrupt them with lavish funerals... They do not promote the benefit of the world.

citations.author: Angus Charles Graham
citations.work: Disputers of the Tao: Philosophical Argument in Ancient China

label: Catalyzed Mencius's defense of innate filial benevolence
description: Mozi's doctrine of universal care alarmed Mencius, who famously denounced Mohism for advocating 'care without distinction' (wu fu, having no father), thereby threatening filial piety and civilized human relationships.
historicalContext: 4th-century BCE intellectual warfare between rival schools in the Warring States period seeking patronage from state rulers.
dialecticalTension: Mencius argued that moral feeling must naturally radiate outward from natural familial affection, whereas Mozi demanded an impartial rational commitment to all humanity.

citations.author: Mencius
citations.quote: Mozi advocated universal love, which is to acknowledge no father... If one acknowledges no father and no ruler, one is a beast.

label: Prefigured utilitarian consequentialism maximizing social welfare and minimizing harm
description: Comparative philosophers highlight Mozi as humanity's first systematic consequentialist, evaluating laws, policies, and morals strictly by whether they promote benefit (li) and eliminate harm (hai) for the greatest number.
historicalContext: The cross-cultural comparative lineage connecting ancient Chinese welfare consequentialism with 19th-century British utilitarianism.
dialecticalTension: Mozi grounded utility in the objective will of Heaven (Tian) and practical material sufficiency, while Bentham formulated it around psychological hedonism.

citations.author: Mozi
citations.quote: The purpose of the benevolent man is to promote what is beneficial to the world and eliminate what is harmful.
